criteria.text: All backend code is Python or Go
All frontend code is TypeScript; no hand-written `.js` / `.jsx` source files
`tsconfig.json` has `"strict": true`

Language toolchain versions pinned: `go` directive and `toolchain` in `go.mod`; `requires-python` in `pyproject.toml` plus `.python-version`; `engines.node` in `package.json` plus `.nvmrc` or `.node-version`
The first paragraph of the README says what the project is and why it exists
The README documents how to get started by opening the Dev Container and running `just setup`, `just run` and `just test`
A licence file is present, or the README states explicitly that the repo is private and unlicensed
Significant design decisions are recorded as ADRs in `docs/adr/`
Projects with more than one component have an architecture overview (diagram or text)
`CHANGELOG.md` is maintained, or release notes are generated from commits
`.gitignore` excludes build output, local environment files and editor files
No build artefacts, generated files or binaries over 1 MB are committed, unless required and documented
The README declares the project status: active, maintained or archived
Layout follows language conventions: Go uses `cmd/<name>/` and `internal/`; Python uses the `src/<package>/` layout with `pyproject.toml`; TypeScript code lives in `src/`
`.editorconfig` present
The default branch is `main`, and it is always in a deployable or releasable state
Commit messages follow Conventional Commits
`main` is protected by a branch ruleset that blocks force-push and requires CI status checks to pass before merge
Releases are tagged with semantic version tags (`vX.Y.Z`)
The commit message format is enforced by a hook or a CI check
A formatter is configured and runs through `just fmt` (for example `gofmt`/`goimports`, `ruff format`, `prettier` or `biome`)
A linter is configured with its config committed, and runs through `just lint` (for example `golangci-lint`, `ruff`, `eslint` or `biome`)
CI runs `just lint`, and a violation fails the build
Pre-commit hooks run the formatter and linter locally
Python static type checking runs in `just lint` in strict mode (`pyright` or `mypy --strict`); TypeScript runs `tsc --noEmit`
Automated tests exist
`just test` runs the full test suite
CI runs the tests on every push and pull request
Critical paths are identified and covered, or line coverage is at least 60%
CI reports coverage, with a threshold that fails the build
External interfaces (APIs, databases, CLIs) have integration or end-to-end tests
GitHub Actions workflows are committed in `.github/workflows/`
CI runs `just check` and `just build` on every push and pull request; workflows call `just` recipes rather than duplicating their commands
The pipeline completes in under 10 minutes
Release and deployment are automated: Fly.io and Cloudflare targets deploy from a workflow; Kubernetes targets publish the image and chart, and ArgoCD syncs them
Every third-party action is pinned to a full commit SHA
Every workflow sets `permissions:` explicitly, with least privilege
No manual step sits between merge and deploy or release
A lockfile is committed: `go.sum`, `uv.lock` (or `poetry.lock`), `package-lock.json` or `pnpm-lock.yaml`
Renovate is configured with `renovate.json` (or `.github/renovate.json5`) and is opening PRs

Renovate covers every ecosystem in the repo: language packages, Dockerfile base images, GitHub Actions, Helm chart dependencies, Dev Container features, and the tool versions pinned in the `justfile`. Renovate has `hostRules` credentials for `dhi.io` so it can update hardened base images

Every dependency is pinned to an exact version: no `^`, `~`, `>=`, `*`, `latest`, bare major tags or unversioned entries. This covers language packages (`==` in `pyproject.toml`; exact versions in `package.json` with `save-exact=true` in `.npmrc`; Go `go.mod` versions are exact by design), Docker image tags, Helm chart dependencies, Dev Container images and features, and tool versions. Renovate sets `rangeStrategy: "pin"`. **Library exception:** published dependency metadata (`pyproject.toml` `dependencies`, `package.json` `dependencies` and `peerDependencies`) uses bounded ranges; dev dependencies and the lockfile are exact
The repo has no unused dependencies
Renovate automerges patch and minor updates once CI passes
Base images are pinned by digest, and Renovate maintains the digests
Git history contains no secrets. Secrets are held in 1Password and injected through External Secrets Operator (Kubernetes), `fly secrets` (Fly.io), or Wrangler secrets (Cloudflare)
Secret scanning runs in CI or in pre-commit (for example `gitleaks`)
CI runs a dependency vulnerability scan: `govulncheck`, `pip-audit`, `npm audit` or Trivy
Containers run as a non-root user, with a read-only root filesystem wherever possible
Credentials, API tokens and service accounts are scoped to least privilege
CI scans container images, and the build fails on any critical vulnerability that has a fix available
`just build` produces the release artefact
Artefacts are versioned with semantic versioning
Container images are tagged with both the version and the commit SHA, and the deployed reference is never `latest`

A multi-stage Dockerfile builds the image, and the final (runtime) stage is `FROM` a Docker Hardened Images runtime variant on `dhi.io`, never a `-dev` variant. Go binaries use `dhi.io/static`; `scratch`, `distroless` and Docker Official Images are not used for the runtime stage. Build stages may use DHI `-dev` variants. CI authenticates to `dhi.io` with a Docker access token held as a GitHub Actions secret. N/A for Cloudflare targets
Builds are reproducible: the same commit produces the same artefact
Code contains no hard-coded hostnames, credentials or environment-specific values
Configuration comes from environment variables or config files
A `justfile` at the repo root defines every recipe that section 2.1 requires for the project type
`.devcontainer/devcontainer.json` is present, and the project builds and its tests pass inside the container
The Dev Container installs `just` and every tool the recipes call, at pinned versions, and `postCreateCommand` runs `just setup`
An example config file is committed (`.env.example` or `config.example.yaml`) that lists every setting
The application validates config at startup, and exits with a clear error if a value is missing or invalid
The deployment target is Fly.io, Cloudflare Pages / Workers, or the local Kubernetes cluster, and the README names it
Target configuration is committed: `fly.toml` for Fly.io; `wrangler.toml` or `wrangler.jsonc` for Cloudflare; a Helm chart in `charts/<app>/` for Kubernetes
Kubernetes only: CI runs `helm lint` and `helm template` on the chart, validating the rendered output with `kubeconform`
Kubernetes only: `Chart.yaml` `version` follows semver and is bumped on every chart change; `appVersion` tracks the application version; the image tag defaults to `appVersion`
Kubernetes only: chart templates set resource requests and limits, `securityContext`, and liveness and readiness probes, all configurable through `values.yaml`
Kubernetes only: an ArgoCD Application references the chart; ArgoCD deploys it, not `helm install` run by hand
Every `values.yaml` key is documented, either with comments or with a generated README such as `helm-docs`
Cloudflare and Fly.io only: preview deployments are created for pull requests
Relational data is stored in PostgreSQL or SQLite. No other relational database is used (for example MySQL or MariaDB)

SQLite, including Cloudflare D1, is used only for lightweight deployments, and the README states that the deployment qualifies. SQLite is also allowed for single-user local state in CLIs and for test fixtures

Schema changes go through versioned migrations committed to the repo, and `just migrate` applies them. Example tools: `goose` or `golang-migrate` for Go, Alembic for Python, `wrangler d1 migrations` for D1
Deployment runs migrations automatically before the new version serves traffic: a Helm `pre-upgrade` hook Job on Kubernetes, `release_command` on Fly.io, or a workflow step on Cloudflare
Every migration has a tested down path, or is documented as forward-only with its recovery procedure
*PostgreSQL only:* the major version is pinned, and is the same in the Dev Container, in CI and in production

*PostgreSQL only:* the connection string comes from `DATABASE_URL`, which is sourced from the secret store. The application uses a connection pool: `pgxpool` for Go, `psycopg_pool` or the SQLAlchemy pool for Python, Hyperdrive for Cloudflare Workers
*PostgreSQL only:* the Dev Container provides PostgreSQL as a Docker Compose service, and integration tests run against a real PostgreSQL instance (that service, or Testcontainers)

*SQLite only:* the database file is on persistent storage, and only one instance can run at a time. On Kubernetes that means a Longhorn PVC, `replicas: 1` and the `Recreate` deployment strategy. On Fly.io it means a Fly volume with the app scaled to one Machine
*SQLite only:* the application sets WAL mode, `busy_timeout` and `foreign_keys = ON` on every connection

*SQLite only:* backups use Litestream, or a scheduled `sqlite3 .backup` or `VACUUM INTO`. The live database file is never copied directly. D1 databases use Time Travel plus a scheduled `wrangler d1 export`
Logs go to stdout/stderr with log levels
Logs are structured: JSON or logfmt (`log/slog` for Go, `structlog` or `logging` with a JSON formatter for Python)
Long-running services expose health (liveness) and readiness endpoints; Cloudflare Workers are N/A
Metrics are exposed in Prometheus format
The repo defines alert rules or dashboards for key failure modes, and failures route to Apprise
The deploy and rollback procedure for the target platform is documented
Stateful data is backed up on a schedule
A backup restore has been tested within the last 6 months, and the date is recorded
A runbook covers the most likely failure modes
`CLAUDE.md` (or an equivalent) is present
The agent file tells the agent to use `just` recipes for build, test, lint and run
The agent file sets out coding conventions and project-specific patterns
The agent file lists the files, directories or operations the agent must not change or run
The agent file is reviewed whenever recipes or conventions change, and its contents match the current repo
